title: Tali Scholars and Malayalam Voices
subtitle: When cannons thundered, Malabar picked up the pen
era: Scholarly and literary life, c. 15th-16th centuries
region: Tali temple at Calicut, Ponnani and Tirur in Malabar
moral: A culture is defended by memory as well as arms.

sources.citation: Zainuddin Makhdoom II, Tuhfat al-Mujahidin, completed 1583
sources.note: Malabar-authored chronicle of the Portuguese struggle and Mappila society.

sources.citation: Thunchaththu Ezhuthachan, Adhyatma Ramayanam Kilippattu and Mahabharatam Kilippattu traditions
sources.note: Core texts in the making of literary Malayalam; dating remains debated.

sources.citation: C. Achyuta Menon, Ezhuthachan and His Age (1940); K.V. Krishna Iyer, Zamorins of Calicut (1938); Sheldon Pollock ed., Literary Cultures in History (2003)
sources.note: Scholarly context for Ezhuthachan, Revathi Pattathanam and source uncertainties.

panels.shot: split-screen wide, stormy sea with distant ships on one side, lamp-lit manuscripts and palm leaves on the other

dialogue.text: On the Zamorin’s coast, as Portuguese guns growl offshore, Zainuddin Makhdoom II and Ezhuthachan turn Malabar itself into a text of memory and resistance.

panels.shot: dawn aerial over Calicut, sweeping from crowded harbor to temple spires

dialogue.text: Calicut in the sixteenth century is not only a merchant city. Behind the smell of pepper and sea salt, its stone courtyards kindle a quieter fire: learning.

panels.shot: low-angle inside Tali temple hall, scholars seated in rows facing a central dais

dialogue.text: Each year, under the Revathi star, the Zamorin’s men summon Sanskrit scholars to Tali. The Pattathanam contest turns a temple into an assembly of minds and memory.

panels.shot: medium shot of an aging scholar reciting, younger scholars listening intently

dialogue.text: Logic, grammar, ritual, law—questions flash and answers clash. The prize is not gold alone, but recognition as Pattar, learned in the Vedic, trusted by the Zamorin’s realm.

panels.shot: slow push-in from Tali temple towards coastline, blending into a wide shot of Ponnani mosque

dialogue.text: South along the same coast, Ponnani rises as another kind of school. Under the Makhdooms, its mosque courtyards thicken with Arabic texts, Malabari voices and debates of law and faith.

panels.shot: medium shot of Zainuddin as a young scholar among students in Ponnani

dialogue.text: Zainuddin Makhdoom II grows in this world of study. He learns hadith and law, hears of distant sultans, and watches Portuguese sails creep closer to Malabar’s inlets.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder close-up on Zainuddin’s hand writing Arabic script on paper

dialogue.text: By the 1570s and 80s, battles with the Portuguese scar the coast. Zainuddin begins to write not only law, but history: the struggle of Malabar’s Muslims, framed in the language of jihad.

panels.shot: dramatic side-angle of Zainuddin presenting a bound manuscript to a Deccan envoy

dialogue.text: He completes Tuhfat al-Mujahidin in 1583, dedicating it to Ali Adil Shah of Bijapur. It is a gift, an exhortation, a chronicle asking Deccan power to answer Malabar’s cry.

panels.shot: close-up on Zainuddin’s thoughtful face, shadowed, with a faint view of ships in the distance

dialogue.text: If we forget these years, our children will forget their duty.

panels.shot: wide shot of a teacher reading from Tuhfat to a circle of Mappila listeners

dialogue.text: Tuhfat is no neutral chronicle. It names the Portuguese as oppressors, recalls battles, praises martyrs, and urges Malabar’s Muslims and their allies toward armed struggle and steadfast faith.

panels.shot: crossfade-style composition: temple scholars on the left, mosque scholars on the right, separated by a thin strip of shoreline

dialogue.text: Two intellectual worlds share the same monsoon winds. Sanskrit at Tali, Arabic-Malayalam at Ponnani—overlapping in geography, distinct in lineage and aims.

panels.shot: evening interior of a modest house in Tirur or nearby, Ezhuthachan seated with palm-leaf and stylus

dialogue.text: Elsewhere along Malabar, another quiet figure shapes its language. Ezhuthachan’s dates are debated, but his voice enters the sixteenth-century air through devotional retellings in Malayalam.

panels.shot: gentle close-up on Ezhuthachan reciting to a small group in kilippattu style

dialogue.text: In Adhyatma Ramayanam and Mahabharatam kilippattu traditions, the parrot’s voice leads listeners into epic tales. The stories are old; the Malayalam cadence, newly made wide and intimate.

panels.shot: overhead shot of Ezhuthachan’s hand writing Malayalam in the evolving script on palm leaf

dialogue.text: Scholars debate the exact dates and details of his life. What stands clear is his role in shaping literary Malayalam, making Sanskritic devotion accessible to everyday speakers of the tongue.

panels.shot: medium shot of common townsfolk listening, some with hands folded, to a reading of Adhyatma Ramayanam

dialogue.text: Now you can hear Rama’s journey in your own words.

panels.shot: symbolic wide shot: sea with warships faintly visible, inland scenes of reading Tuhfat and kilippattu side by side

dialogue.text: While cannon smoke hangs over the sea, Malabar’s coast hums with words. Some texts call for armed resistance; others call hearts inward through devotion. All work on memory.

panels.shot: library-like montage of manuscripts: Tuhfat, Sanskrit palm leaves, Malayalam kilippattu, stacked together

dialogue.text: Later ages will catalogue and argue: which year, which patron, which text first. Yet the sixteenth century’s coastline already holds a multilingual archive of how Malabar saw itself.

panels.shot: modern-day low-angle of Tali temple gopuram and Ponnani mosque minaret in the distance, under the same sky

dialogue.text: Today, the stones of Tali and Ponnani stand quiet. Their old contests and classes remind us that Malabar’s battles were fought with ships and steel, but also with stories and chronicles.

panels.shot: final contemplative shot of Zainuddin and Ezhuthachan as statues or imagined figures, surrounded by floating verses

dialogue.text: In their different tongues, Zainuddin and Ezhuthachan show a coast under siege choosing to remember itself. A culture is defended by memory as much as by arms, and its strongest citadel is the word.
